https://whbl.com/2026/08/02/hungary-pm-f.text: Sign In Search NEWS WEATHER EVENTS OBITUARIES CLOSINGS MORE AGRICULTURE BLOGS LOCAL SPORTS ON AIR PODCASTS Hungary PM flags “critical” days ahead with looming nuclear shutdown By Thomson Reuters Aug 2, 2026 | 5:43 AM BUDAPEST, Aug 2 (Reuters) – Hungary faces a critical five days, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday, as the drying out of the Danube forces the country’s sole ​nuclear power plant to shut for the first time in ‌over four decades, with a new heatwave looming. Large parts of Europe have been hit by prolonged heat and drought, lowering river levels and raising concerns about water supplies, river transport and power generation. Hungary’s 2 gigawatt Paks power ‌plant, ​which runs four Russian-built reactors, was operating ⁠at just over 10% of ⁠its total capacity on Sunday after the Danube, whose waters it uses as a coolant, fell to a record low. The water authority was projecting that the level of the river, ​which flows from Germany to the Black Sea, would drop further in the coming days. “We are facing the most critical five ⁠days ahead,” Magyar said in a ⁠Facebook video. “Tomorrow, the Paks power plant will not be ​generating, while the hottest, 40-degree (Celsius, 104 Fahrenheit) days are ahead. “The power ​grid, our public services and ourselves will all come ‌under enormous strain,” said Magyar, who has warned that Paks could remain idle for weeks. Falls in water levels have also disrupted shipping and tourism in Hungary and triggered water-use restrictions in more than ⁠100 cities and villages, including on the outskirts of Budapest, according to government records. Magyar reiterated a call for companies, public institutions, local governments and ⁠households to significantly ‌reduce or reschedule electricity use during evening peak ⁠hours between 5 p.m. and 10 p.m. The government ​will ‌decide on Sunday whether to apply mandatory electricity ​use restrictions ⁠for large companies from Monday, he said. The crisis could cost Hungary 100 billion to 200 billion forints ($315 million to $630 million) due to the surging price of imported electricity, Mark Radnai, vice chairman of Magyar’s Tisza party, said on Facebook. ($1 = 316.3700 forints) (Reporting by Gergely Szakacs; Editing ​by Kevin Liffey) Comments Leave a Reply Cancel reply You must be logged in to post a comment. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjkg.text: Image source, Metinvest/Zaporizhstal Image caption, After one attack on the Zaporizhzhia steelworks, a blast furnace was restarted only for the site to be hit again hours later By Vitaly Shevchenko Chief Analyst, BBC Monitoring Published 3 hours ago Like thousands of other residents of Zaporizhzhia, Denys Maksyshko has spent years working for local steel factory Zaporizhstal. For generations, it has been the biggest and richest source of employment in this major Ukrainian city. "Zaporizhstal is not just a big company, it's the heart of the city," he says. Now, following a series of Russian missile strikes, this heart has stopped beating. The huge factory that employs 8,500 people shut down indefinitely after four waves of Russian attacks - two in August, and two in September. "All the equipment has been almost completely destroyed. There are no windows left, and there are holes in the roofs. The blast furnaces have been almost completely ruined," Maksyshko complains. Russia fired a total of 17 missiles at Zaporizhstal, according to Oleksandr Myronenko, chief operating officer of steelworks owner Metinvest. Eight workers were killed and 31 wounded. "We're now clearing rubble and trying to plan recovery," Myronenko tells the BBC. At the moment it is far from certain Zaporizhstal will ever start up again. Image source, Metinvest/Zaporizhstal Image caption, The Zaporizhstal works has been hit by four waves of Russian attacks Russia's persistent campaign of air strikes against Ukrainian metallurgical plants started in August. By now, all of them have been hit, some several times. This is a key sector of the Ukrainian economy, and naturally an attractive target for Russia. Before the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's GDP and a third of its exports. It provided employment for more than half a million people, and every 13th job in Ukraine was linked to the industry one way or another. Because of the recent Russian attacks, it has all but ground to a halt and its contribution to Ukraine's GDP now "is probably close to zero", says Myronenko. Until recently his company was Ukraine's biggest producer of steel and iron, but all its steelworks are for now out of action. "Clearly, they're trying to stop Ukraine's economy and stop Ukraine from getting [export] money from abroad, from paying taxes and wages, from ensuring that cities live and people have jobs," says Myronenko. "Their efforts have been very effective so far." The damage to the metals industry could have devastating consequences for Ukraine's economy and society. Ukraine had 12 metallurgical plants before losing parts of its industrial heartland in the east shortly after the start of hostilities with Russia in 2014. By 2018, there were just nine, and three years into the full-scale war in 2025 that number had fallen to six. Among those lost were the Azovstal and Illich plants in Mariupol, Ukraine's south-eastern city captured after a months-long Russian siege. Among the steel-making cities caught up in Russia's recent missile campaign is President Volodymyr Zelensky's home city of Kryvyi Rih. On 25 September, Ukraine's biggest steelworks, Arcelor Mittal Kryvyi Rih, announced it was unable to reopen after repeated attacks over five weeks, praising the bravery of its workers, five of whom had died. Latest on war in Ukraine Russia targeting 'ordinary life' with attacks on Ukraine's data centres, Zelensky says Published 4 days ago Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water Published 6 days ago Cultural treasures are being destroyed worldwide - so why is no-one being punished? Published 20 September Local Defence Council head Oleksandr Vilkul issued an emergency address to the city's residents, in which he spoke of a "very serious blow" that would affect more than just thousands of jobs. The situation, he admitted, was very difficult. "It is taxes feeding into our community's budget," he said. "They provided funds for keeping the city's infrastructure running, repairing heating plants and their pipes, funds for nursery schools, social services and many other things." Taxes paid by metal-making companies have funded 30-70% of local government spending in their host cities, says Stanislav Zinchenko, head of Kyiv-based consultancy GMK Center. "In other words, the physical survival of these cities depended on these companies," he told the BBC. "This is a catastrophic problem for Ukraine's economy. Before the war, the mining and metallurgical industry was a key industry," he told the BBC. "It was always the biggest investor in the economy, investing $2bn-$3bn (Â£1.5bn-Â£2.3bn) a year on average." Image source, Metinvest/Zaporizhstal Image caption, Even if production were to resume, it would not be business as usual at Zaporizhstal any time soon If the steelworks remain shut, hundreds of thousands of people may lose their jobs, and the resulting waves of migration will reach far beyond Ukraine, Zinchenko warned. "A humanitarian catastrophe is looming." The end of steelmaking in Ukraine would also have severe consequences for its defence capabilities and reconstruction. Steel is vital for producing military equipment, as well as for making shelters and repairing countless buildings damaged by Russia. Russia has justified its attacks on the steel plants for that reason, alleging that the plants in Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih were all producing military hardware. "We attempted relaunching Zaporizhstal. We restarted a furnace, and it worked for 10 hours before there was another air strike," Oleksandr Vodoviz of Metinvest told a conference in Kyiv. There was no point yet on spending money on recovery as the situation was unclear, he added. Even if production were to resume, it would not be business as usual for Ukrainian steelmakers any time soon. Russian attacks on railways have made transporting their products within Ukraine difficult and dangerous, and strikes against ports have turned exports into a lethal lottery. "Ports have essentially been blocked," said Oleksandr Myronenko. "Every ship is at risk of being attacked, and their chances are 50-50 - either you make it, or you don't." EU quotas on steel imports introduced on 1 July may compound the problems faced by Ukraine. But Denys Maksyshko, the Zaporizhstal worker, remains upbeat. His colleagues are doing their bit to revive the factory, clearing away rubble and fixing whatever can be fixed. "This is similar to what the military do in the trenches. Ordinary people are fighting to keep the factory alive like soldiers." https://www.dw.com/en/russia-denies-anti.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NrFa The woman who died worked at an anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region Image: The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Russia denied claims that it was imposing anti-plague measures following the death of a laboratory technician of pneumonic plague. The woman worked at the anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region. The authorities in Russia, however, said the cause of death is yet to be confirmed, and Moscow's health authority Rospotrebnadzor has denied claims the country had put special measures in place. Authorities deny reports of plague According to Rospotrebnadzor, the information "does not originate from official sources" and is "untrue," with Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev adding that the inspection had found that the woman's death was a result of pneumonia. "No microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples," he said. Plague is a disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, known to be the most contagious and potentially fatal if not treated early. Some reports in Russia suggested the woman could have caught the disease from a broken test tube, while others speculated on a potential link between her death and a lab accident at the institute. The woman may have come into contact with up to 200 people, all of whom are under quarantine, according to one report. Irkutsk is at low risk, according to the World Health Organization Image: Kirill Kukhmar/TASS/picture alliance World Health Organization monitoring situation The World Health Organization (WHO) said the information it had received from Russia suggests that "no case" of the disease has so far been recorded in Irkutsk. Russia has launched an epidemiological investigation into a case of pneumonia, labeled as "community acquired," in an employee at the Irkutsk Institute. "Test results showed no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens" in the people who came into contact with the person, the WHO said, adding that the agency estimates the risk to be "moderate to low" for Irkutsk. The WHO is still monitoring the situation closely, it said. US President Donald Trump said he will discuss the case with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump also said the US intelligence is in "very deep discussions" on the matter, while also calling the disease "rough." "That's a disease we used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They’re like an army,” the US president told reporters at the White House . US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington is monitoring the situation. According to Rubio, Russia needs to "share more information with the world." Photograph: Diannie Chavez/The Republic/USA TODAY Network/Reuters Connect Arizona Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while trying to repair campaign sign Bernadette Greene-Placentia says she is sharing her story in order to fight for victims of sexual assault Sam Levin in Los Angeles Wed 7 Oct 2026 16.21 EDT Last modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 16.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google This article contains graphic descriptions of sexual assault. A congressional candidate in Arizona says she was attacked and raped in August while trying to repair one of her damaged campaign signs. Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a trucker and small-business owner, shared her account with the Phoenix New Times , a local publication. The assault took place on 14 August, according to the campaign. The Democratic candidate, running in a district that includes parts of Phoenix, told the newspaper that she was walking across a parking lot just after 2am to fix a campaign sign when an attacker smashed her over the head, causing her to black out. Greene-Placentia told the newspaper that she awoke to find a man on top of her and discovered he was raping her. She recalled another man coming over and pushing her leg, at which point she said she swung her foot at him. The man said, “Not even worth it”, and the two attackers left, leaving her face down in the parking lot, she recalled. The candidate said her memory of the incident and its aftermath was hazy, telling the newspaper she did not remember picking herself off the pavement or returning home. “It’s just these little tiny flashes of things that I do remember,” Greene-Placentia told the Phoenix New Times. “As much as I don’t want to remember, I’ve tried very, very hard to remember more stuff. But that’s where I’m at.” She said she may have had a concussion as a result of the attack and that her body was covered in bruises. She said she initially wanted to forget what had happened and felt “embarrassed”, at first choosing not to report the assault. But she told the paper that on the campaign trail, she often spoke about fighting for Arizonans, “and I didn’t feel like I could keep saying that if I weren’t also fighting for women that are victims of sexual assault”. Greene-Placentia told her campaign staff and husband about the assault days after it happened and reported it to the Maricopa county sheriff’s office two weeks later, according to the Phoenix New Times. The newspaper interviewed Greene-Placentia’s relatives, friends, campaign staff and landlord about the aftermath of the assault. “Speaking publicly about what happened has been incredibly difficult for Bernadette,” a campaign spokesperson told the Guardian on Wednesday after the Phoenix New Times story was published. “She chose to share her story because she knows many survivors struggle in silence, and she hopes that by speaking about her experience, others will know they are not alone.” The spokesperson added: “She hopes the focus remains on supporting survivors and making sure people who have experienced sexual violence know they are seen, heard and supported.” “I need to let women know that it’s OK to talk about it,” Greene-Placentia told the newspaper. Stephanie Simacek, a state representative and friend of Greene-Placentia, said the congressional candidate told her of the assault in early September, telling the Phoenix New Times, “I felt sick to my stomach, and it was extremely disturbing. It was a big wake-up call for me. I think oftentimes, as candidates and electeds, we think that it’s not going to happen to us.” A Maricopa county sheriff’s spokesperson declined to comment, saying the investigation was ongoing. Greene-Placentia is running against an incumbent Republican member of Congress, Abraham Hamadeh. Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). https://www.politico.eu/article/krakow-s.text: A Polish man, who fatally shot six people after driving onto Kraków’s main square Saturday, died in hospital Monday, local police reported. “We would like to inform you that the perpetrator of the tragic events died in hospital early this morning,” police wrote on X . The masked 24-year-old opened fire on passersby in central Kraków, killing six people, including a British citizen, and injuring 16 — 12 of whom remain in critical condition. Police shot and detained the attacker. They also found his parents and sister dead at their family home Sunday. Investigators are examining those deaths alongside the Kraków attack, and have opened a terrorism probe . Advertisement Advertisement Authorities identified the suspect as Michał O., from Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a town about 140 kilometers northeast of Kraków. He had a firearms permit and was not previously known to police. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński initially said that “everything indicated that he was fascinated by extreme right-wing ideologies,” but later he said the shooter’s motives remained unclear. “My deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims of the tragic attack in Kraków. My highest praise for the heroic police officers who risked their lives,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on X on Saturday . “And a heartfelt appeal to politicians of all stripes: do not exploit this tragedy. We will establish all the circumstances of this crime.”
